clue.text: Purchase money always available on time

parts.note: L stands for pound, from the Latin libra, a unit of money
ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'
an age is a long stretch of time

explanation.surface: Someone describes ready cash that is always to hand when a payment falls due.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purchase' is not buying here but grip or mechanical advantage; 'available on' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Purchase in its mechanical sense is a firm hold giving advantage, the same idea as the force gained with a lever.

clue.text: Predominant type found in newspaper production

definitions.text: Predominant type found in newspaper production

parts.words: Predominant type found in newspaper production
parts.note: 'type' reads as printing type, but it is the kind of person who dominates the making of a newspaper

explanation.surface: A print-room remark about which typeface dominates the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' suggests fonts in the print room; the clue means the person who runs the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The person in charge of a newspaper's content is its dominant figure, the chief of the whole production.

clue.text: Not inclined to build

definitions.meaning: standing straight up rather than leaning or sloping
to put up or construct, as a building

explanation.surface: Someone is unwilling to do any construction work.
explanation.definitionFit: Upright means not sloping, and to put up a structure is to construct it; both senses belong to the one word.

clue.text: Dogs set about assailant

indicators.note: to set about something is to tackle or rework it, so the following word's letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Guard dogs are turned loose on an attacker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set about' reads as attack, which suits the dogs, but it signals rearranging ASSAILANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Alsatian is the British name for the German shepherd breed of dog.

clue.text: Fugitive takes cover in English diocese

indicators.note: in places the word for cover inside the word for diocese

parts.note: a see is the area under a bishop, a diocese
a cap is a covering, as on a bottle or the head

explanation.surface: A runaway hides out within an English bishop's territory.
explanation.walkthrough: A see is the district governed by a bishop, a convention worth knowing; 'takes' is only a joining word here.
explanation.definitionFit: A fugitive is someone who has fled, typically from prison, which is what an escaped person is.

clue.text: Temporary fault makes light go out around China's capital

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit around the next piece, enclosing it
letters that go out of their order are scattered, so the word light is rearranged
the capital of a word is its first letter, here of China

explanation.surface: A brief power cut causes the lights to fail around Beijing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go out' suits a light failing, but it rearranges LIGHT into GLITH, which goes around the C from 'China's capital'.
explanation.definitionFit: A glitch is a brief malfunction or hiccup in a system, a passing fault rather than a lasting one.

clue.text: Traveller in pain on small yacht's prow

parts.note: gyp is informal British slang for pain or discomfort
S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: a prow is the front of a boat, so this takes the opening letter of yacht

explanation.surface: A passenger aboard a little yacht feels unwell at the bow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prow' picks the first letter of 'yacht's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Traveller is a common British term for members of itinerant communities, which this word also names.

clue.text: Broken-down train isn't moving

indicators.note: something broken down is taken apart, so the letters of the following words are reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A failed train is stuck on the line.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface says the train is stationary, while the answer means the opposite: on the move.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in transit is on its way between places, in motion rather than at rest.

clue.text: Pass — one is to be shown going round settlements

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass, a gap between peaks

indicators.note: letters going round are churned about, so the words one is are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction that a mountain pass must be shown circling some villages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going round' rearranges ONE IS into ONIES; 'to be shown' is only link material.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonies are settlements founded by people from another country, or outposts held abroad.

clue.text: They sit qualifications

definitions.meaning: people on horseback or bicycles sit astride their mounts
conditions or provisos added to a statement or contract

explanation.surface: Candidates sit exams to gain their certificates.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests sitting exams for qualifications; in fact horse-mounted people sit, and added provisos qualify a statement.
explanation.definitionFit: Equestrians sit in the saddle, and a clause added to a bill or statement qualifies it.

clue.text: Head south for the big cities

parts.note: a capital is the head or top part of a column in architecture
S is the compass abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: An instruction to drive south toward the major cities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head south' reads as a direction to travel; 'Head' is the top of a column, a capital.
explanation.definitionFit: A capital is a country's or region's chief city, so the plural names the leading cities.

clue.text: Twelve-inch pace?

parts.note: twelve inches make a measured foot and a pace is a step, so the clue describes a stride literally

explanation.surface: A query about a stride exactly a foot long.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads the answer literally as a foot-length unit plus a stride.
explanation.definitionFit: A single stride made in walking is one tread, and the clue playfully measures it by the foot.

clue.text: Longs for time with game partners

parts.note: a year is a period of time
in bridge, North and South play as partners, N and S
in bridge, North and South play as partners, N and S

explanation.surface: Someone pines for the chance to play a game with their regular partners.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge the four players are named by compass points, and North and South partner each other.
explanation.definitionFit: To long for something is to desire it ardently, the same as pining or craving.

clue.text: Production line that's quietly effective?

parts.note: 'production line' suggests a factory, but it is a line in a stage production delivered softly yet heard by the audience

explanation.surface: A query about a factory assembly line that runs efficiently and silently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Production line' pretends to be manufacturing; the production is a play.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor's hushed aside meant to carry to the audience is a theatrical line spoken softly that still reaches the back row.

clue.text: Got quickly to one's feet — or didn't make a move?

definitions.meaning: rose to standing rapidly, reading fast as speedy
stayed firmly in place, fast meaning fixed

explanation.surface: A puzzled question whether someone leapt up or stayed motionless.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is the two meanings of 'fast': quick and firmly fixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast can mean speedy or immovable, so the phrase covers rising quickly and refusing to budge.

clue.text: Classified government order

parts.note: 'classified' suggests secret, but here means graded into ranks, and the word's ending -archy means rule or government

explanation.surface: A secret directive issued by the state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classified' suggests top secret; it means arranged by rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A system of ranked levels is an order sorted by grade, and many such systems are forms of rule.

clue.text: Short of cash in inn, I'd get thrown out

indicators.note: letters thrown out of order are jumbled, so the words inn, I'd and get are rearranged

parts.note: the apostrophe is dropped, leaving the letters I and D

explanation.surface: A penniless drinker fears being ejected from the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrown out' suits a broke customer, but it signals rearranging INN, ID and GET.
explanation.definitionFit: Being needy means lacking money for the necessities of life, the plight of the very poor.

clue.text: Emphatic about corporal, say, being out of step

indicators.note: the word for emphatic goes about, wrapping, the soldier's abbreviation

parts.note: insistent means emphatic, firmly demanding
a corporal is an example of a non-commissioned officer, NCO

explanation.surface: A forceful drill corporal is marching out of time with the squad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks the corporal as one example of an NCO.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out of step means not in agreement or harmony, which is what lacking constancy describes.

clue.text: They get stuck into pieces of meat

definitions.text: They get stuck into pieces of meat

parts.words: They get stuck into pieces of meat
parts.note: 'get stuck into' suggests hungry diners tucking in, but it is the literal pushing of spikes through meat

explanation.surface: Hungry diners tucking into their food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get stuck into' is British slang for eating heartily; read literally it is about spikes.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal or wooden spikes for kebabs are pushed through chunks of meat for grilling.

clue.text: Make safe and secure, possibly

indicators.note: possibly says the following word may be arranged another way, signalling a reordering of its letters

explanation.surface: Instructions for making a place safe and locked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secure' looks like part of the definition beside 'safe', but it is the letters reordered.
explanation.definitionFit: To save someone from danger is to bring them out of harm's way.

clue.text: His cricket records still stand today

definitions.text: His cricket records still stand today

parts.words: His cricket records still stand today
parts.note: sounds like a batsman's unbeaten scores, but means the annual cricket almanac named after its founder

explanation.surface: A tribute to a cricketer whose batting records remain unbeaten.
explanation.walkthrough: The famous yearly almanac of cricket statistics was founded in 1864 by the player John Wisden and is still published.
explanation.definitionFit: The founder's name lives on in the yearly almanac, so his records of the game literally still sit on shelves.

clue.text: I pry about that racket

indicators.note: the word for pry goes about, enclosing, the letter I

parts.note: to nose is to pry or snoop

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to snooping into the source of a din.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a loud din or uproar, any unwelcome loud sound.

clue.text: Issued with name and date corrected

indicators.note: something corrected is put right, so the letters of the two words are set in a new order

explanation.surface: A document went out after its name and date were amended.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue from a source is to flow or come out of it, as light from a lamp.

clue.text: One wasn't there to provide such a defence

definitions.text: One wasn't there to provide such a defence

parts.words: One wasn't there to provide such a defence
parts.note: the clue describes the plea of having been elsewhere when a crime took place

explanation.surface: A defendant was absent and so could offer no defence.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests nobody turned up to defend; in fact absence is the defence itself.
explanation.definitionFit: This plea claims the accused was somewhere else when the offence was committed.

clue.text: Reserve short time in holiday place

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation inside the word for the holiday place

parts.note: the seaside is a classic British holiday destination
T is the standard short form of time

explanation.surface: A brief stay is booked at a resort.
explanation.definitionFit: To reserve something is to keep it back for later use, putting it to one side.

clue.text: Embrace to really fix things

definitions.meaning: a tight hug, as between lovers or boxers
to settle a deal or argument conclusively

explanation.surface: A hug is offered as a way of truly making amends.
explanation.definitionFit: A tight hug is one sense, and settling a deal decisively, as in sealing it, is the other.

clue.text: Liberty, for example

parts.note: 'Liberty' reads as freedom, but is the famous sculpture in New York harbour

explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberty' looks abstract; it is the monument, so the answer is a sculpted figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The Statue of Liberty is a well-known example of a sculpted monumental figure.

clue.text: One starts with a high jump, then performs acrobatic feats

definitions.text: One starts with a high jump, then performs acrobatic feats

parts.words: One starts with a high jump, then performs acrobatic feats
parts.note: 'high jump' suggests an athletics event, but it is a leap from an aircraft followed by stunts in freefall

explanation.surface: An athlete opens with the high jump and moves on to gymnastics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High jump' pretends to be the track-and-field event.
explanation.definitionFit: A parachutist who leaps from a plane and performs freefall manoeuvres before opening the canopy fits the description.
